analysis.one_liner: Removes dollar caps on damages for victims of workplace discrimination.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have removed dollar caps on damages for victims of job discrimination, was introduced in January 1995 and never advanced past subcommittee referral.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law caps the money a worker can win in a lawsuit for intentional job discrimination, and the caps differ depending on the type of discrimination: a 1991 law set a separate, different cap for cases of racial discrimination in employment. This bill would have removed all those dollar caps so that any victim of intentional workplace discrimination could recover the full damages a jury finds, and it would have guaranteed a jury trial for either side in these cases. The bill never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face intentional discrimination on the job — including discrimination based on race, sex, religion, or disability — would gain the ability to recover unlimited compensatory and punitive damages. Under the 1991 law being amended, Black victims faced a different cap than other victims; this bill would have removed all the caps and equalized remedies for everyone.

how_it_helps.text: It removes the dollar caps on compensatory and punitive damages for victims of intentional employment discrimination, allowing awards proportionate to actual harm.
It eliminates the unequal treatment under which Black victims of discrimination faced a separate cap from other victims, giving all discrimination victims the same legal remedies.
It guarantees any party in these cases the right to a jury trial.

analysis.who_pays: Employers found liable for intentional discrimination would face potentially unlimited damages awards, including punitive damages, instead of the fixed caps set in 1991.

drawbacks.text: Employers would face uncapped compensatory and punitive damages for intentional discrimination, raising the financial risk of doing business and the cost of defending lawsuits.
The caps being removed were themselves a compromise from the Civil Rights Act of 1991, designed to limit litigation exposure; removing them fully removes that negotiated limit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest in reach: it would have removed dollar caps that leave low-compensation discrimination victims undercompensated, and it would have ended a race-based double standard in the law. The cost is that employers, including small businesses, could face larger damages awards, which critics argued would raise the price of defending even weak claims. On balance it was a straightforward civil rights fix whose main drawback was increased litigation exposure for employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to House committees and subcommittees in early 1995 and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 4, 1995, the first days of the new Republican-led Congress, and referred to the House Judiciary and Economic and Educational Opportunities Committees.
On January 25 and February 1, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution and the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, where it remained.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in the 104th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, whose potential liability for discrimination damages stayed capped, benefited from the bill's death; workers who face discrimination remained subject to the existing dollar limits and the old race-based double standard.

for.name: Barbara Kennelly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to equalize and lift caps on discrimination damages.

for.name: 24 of 198 House Democrats and 2 of 234 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (26 total, nearly all Democrats).

for.name: Business and employer groups
for.what_they_did: Opposed uncapped discrimination damages; employer-side groups generally opposed lifting the 1991 caps.

sides.party_line_note: 26 of the 27 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; only 2 of the 234 House Republicans signed on, and the bill died in a House now controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: Removing damage caps would raise their potential liability in intentional-discrimination cases. Businesses opposed uncapped damages because juries could impose large awards.
